transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, it's... I suppose I'm here because of an ongoing situation at my agency, which has been incredibly stressful. I'm a translator and an interpreter, you see. I do a lot of high-stakes corporate and legal work—I have my master's degree in this, so precision is absolutely everything in my field. You have to be meticulous. But for months now—literally going back to at least October of last year—I’ve been seeing this exact same pattern in our project files, and it's getting to the point where I had to talk to someone about the stress of it all. 

We use this localized software with a shared translation memory, which is essentially a database that stores segments of text we've previously translated and approved. But lately, certain subcontractors, along with one specific colleague of mine who handles the secondary reviews, they keep going in and making these tiny, almost imperceptible changes to the translation memory. And it’s not just the terminology they're messing with. They are actually manipulating the timestamps on the backend. They do it specifically so that when the final export is generated, it looks exactly like my quality control failed. Like I was the one who approved a substandard, error-filled translation. 

I took it to the IT department, obviously, because I document everything. I showed them the discrepancies. But IT ran their little diagnostics and they claim the audit trail is completely
Do you believe your colleague and those subcontractors are deliberately trying to sabotage you?

Well, yes. I mean, what other logical conclusion could there possibly be? You have to understand, I wouldn't just jump to something like that lightly. My professional reputation is on the line. But I’m here, sitting in this office talking to you, precisely because for months—literally month after month—I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It’s not an accident. It’s always the same subcontractors, and it's always funneled through this one specific colleague of mine. 

They go into the translation memory
Have there been times recently when you felt unusually energized or high, like you needed much less sleep than usual?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, energized? High? No. If anything, I’m exhausted. You would be too, if you had to spend every waking hour meticulously double-checking every single segment of text you’ve ever touched, just to make sure someone hasn’t gone in and subtly altered a phrasing or, or worse, messed with the backend timestamps again. I sleep, you know, when I can, but it’s not because I don’t *want* to sleep or because I feel like I don’t need it. I absolutely need it. I need my rest to maintain the level of precision required for my job, especially with all this going on. 

It’s just that the stress of it all, the constant vigilance required to protect my professional reputation from this... this coordinated effort to undermine me... it takes a toll. So, no, I haven’t felt unusually energized at all. Quite the opposite, really. I’m just trying to keep my head above water and make sure my work, my actual work, isn't being compromised by these people. It's a full-time job on top of my actual full-time job, just monitoring the translation memory for these unauthorized changes. So, sleep is definitely something I want, not something I feel I can just skip because I'm feeling 'high' or whatever you called it.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

No. No, definitely not. I mean, I know why you're asking that—people always assume that if you're experiencing a coordinated... situation, like I am, that it must be because you're hallucinating or hearing things. But I assure you, my hearing is perfectly fine, and I only hear people when they are actually speaking to me. In my line of work, auditory processing is absolutely critical. When I'm doing simultaneous interpretation, for instance, I have to listen to the speaker in one language, process it, and speak it in another language with a delay of maybe two or three seconds. If I were hearing voices that weren't there, I wouldn't be able to do my job. It would be a complete disaster. 

The things I'm dealing with, the sabotage, it's all documented in the project files, in the translation memory. It's visual, it's digital, it's in the timestamps. It's not some... phantom voice whispering in my ear. It's my colleague, sitting three desks down, quietly logging into the system and altering the localized strings. It's the subcontractors sending back files with microscopic errors inserted into the text. So, no, no voices. Just the very real, very tangible stress of having to constantly audit my own software to prove I'm not the one making these mistakes.
If someone showed you clear proof that no one at work had altered the files, would you believe it?

Well, see, that’s the thing. "Clear proof" is a very subjective term in this context. I mean, you say "clear proof," but what does that actually look like when you're dealing with a system as complex as enterprise-level localization software? Because, let me tell you, I’ve had this exact conversation with our IT department. I went to them, I sat down with the lead systems administrator—a guy who, frankly, should know better—and I asked him to pull the server logs. I wanted the raw data, the unedited audit trail of every single keystroke and commit made to the repository over the last six months. 

And you know what he showed me? He showed me a screen that looked... clean. Too clean, honestly. He pointed to the timestamps and the user IDs and said, "Look, there's no record of anyone else accessing these segments after you approved them." But that’s exactly the problem! That’s what I’ve been trying to explain to management, and now to you. The fact that the audit trail looks clean isn't proof that nothing happened; it's proof of how sophisticated this operation is. 

I know what I’m seeing in those project files. I’m here because for months—literally months—I’ve been tracking this pattern. It’s always certain subcontractors, and it's always this one specific colleague of mine. They go in, they make these tiny, almost imperceptible changes to the translation memory—swapping a comma for a semicolon, altering a backend timestamp by three seconds—just enough to trigger an error flag in the automated quality assurance check. And they do it in a way that makes it look like my quality control failed. 

So, when IT tells me the audit trail is clean, I don't feel relieved. I feel terrified, because it means they’ve figured out a way to scrub their digital footprints. They’ve arranged the record, the actual server data, to ensure the blame falls squarely on me. It's a complete manipulation of the system. So, no, if someone handed me a piece of paper or showed me a screen that supposedly proved no one altered the files, I wouldn't believe it. I couldn't. Because I know what the files looked like when I saved them, and I know what they look like when the client receives them, and those two things do not match. The evidence is in the discrepancies, not in the supposedly "clean" logs that someone has obviously tampered with to cover their tracks.
Have you been feeling persistently depressed or down most of the day?

No, I wouldn't say depressed. I mean, it's a very specific word, isn't it? Depressed. It implies a sort of... giving up, a lack of motivation, a feeling of hopelessness. And I am certainly not hopeless, and I definitely haven't given up. If anything, I'm more motivated than ever, because I have to be. I mean, when you're dealing with the level of scrutiny and... and just blatant sabotage that I am, you don't have time to be depressed. You have to be alert. 

Now, am I down? Well, yes, of course I'm down sometimes. I think anyone would be feeling a bit down if they were in my position. It's incredibly disheartening. You spend years, decades even, building a reputation in this industry. Simultaneous interpretation, especially at the level I work at, it requires a pristine track record. You are the voice of diplomats, of CEOs. Trust is everything. And to see that trust being systematically chipped away by these... these fabricated errors, these manipulated translation memories... it’s frustrating. It’s infuriating, really. 

So, I wouldn't say I'm persistently depressed most of the day. I'm busy most of the day. I'm working my regular hours, and then I'm spending hours after that running my own manual diffs on the repository, comparing my local backups to the server versions, trying to catch them in the act before the files go to the client. It’s exhausting, like I said before, and it certainly doesn't put me in a cheerful mood. There are moments, usually late at night when I'm staring at a screen full of code and trying to figure out how they managed to alter a string without leaving a trace in the logs, where I just feel this profound sense of... isolation. Because nobody believes me. Management thinks I'm making excuses for sloppy work, IT thinks I don't understand how the system works, and my colleague—the one who's actually doing this—just sits there smiling at me in the breakroom. 

So, yes, it brings me down. It’s a heavy burden to carry, knowing that your livelihood is under attack and you are the only one who sees it. But it's not depression. It's a very rational, completely justified reaction to a highly stressful and unfair situation. I don't need antidepressants, Doctor. I need a secure server environment and an independent audit of the localization team's workflow. That's what would make me feel better.
Has anything happened that made you think your coworkers can control your computer or files in a way that seems impossible to other people?

Impossible? No, no, I think... I think you might be misunderstanding the mechanics of what I'm dealing with here. I'm not suggesting anything impossible, or... or supernatural, or whatever it is you might be implying. I don't think they're controlling my computer with their minds or using some sort of sci-fi hacking tool. That would be absurd. Everything they are doing, every single alteration to those files, is completely grounded in the reality of how enterprise networks operate. 

I mean, if you understand how a translation management system works—we use a very standard, industry-wide platform—you'd know that it's all networked. It's all connected to the company's central servers. It is not "impossible" for someone to access my files; it's actually frighteningly easy if you have the right permissions or if you've managed to bypass the security protocols. My colleague, the one I mentioned earlier, he doesn't need to do anything impossible. He just needs to wait until I step away to get a coffee, or... or perhaps he's using a remote desktop protocol. Maybe he got hold of my login credentials, or maybe someone in IT—who, as we've established, is already turning a blind eye to the altered logs—gave him backdoor administrative access. 

So, when you say "impossible to other people," I have to assume you mean people who just don't understand basic IT infrastructure. Because to a systems administrator, or to anyone who actually works in digital localization, what's happening to my files is perfectly explainable. It's unauthorized network access, plain and simple. It's malicious, yes. It's highly coordinated, absolutely. But impossible? No. I've never claimed they were doing anything outside the bounds of normal, albeit highly unethical, computer usage. They're just exploiting the system's vulnerabilities and... and using very standard tools to alter the text strings and then scrub the metadata. There's no magic involved, Doctor, just a very calculated effort to ruin my professional reputation.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being put into your mind, taken out, or broadcast so other people could know them?

What? No, no, absolutely not. I feel like... I feel like we’re veering off into a completely different territory here, Doctor. My thoughts are entirely my own. I mean, think about it—I’m an interpreter. I have a graduate degree in this, I’ve spent years training my brain to listen to one language, process the syntax and the cultural nuance, and simultaneously output it in another language. My cognitive function, my... my mental architecture, if you will, is my most valuable asset. If someone were somehow putting thoughts into my head or taking them out, I wouldn't be able to do my job for three minutes, let alone sit in a booth for a three-hour corporate summit. 

And as for broadcasting my thoughts so other people could know them? I mean, how would that even work? Biologically, physically, it makes absolutely no sense. I'm a rational person. The people who are trying to undermine me at work—my colleague, those subcontractors—they don't need to read my mind or broadcast my thoughts to know what I'm doing. They don't need telepathy. They just need access to the company's localization servers. They just need to monitor my commit history on the repository. Why on earth would they bother with something impossible like mind-reading when they can just log into the translation management system and see exactly what I’m working on? 

So, no, I have never felt anything like that. My mind is perfectly clear, my thoughts are secure, and my memory of exactly how I left those files is pristine. The tampering is happening on the network, on the hard drives, not inside my head. I really need you to understand that distinction, because asking me about... about thought broadcasting just tells me that you're still not grasping the technical reality of the sabotage I'm actually dealing with.
Aside from the situation at work, have you become less interested in seeing other people or doing your usual activities?

Less interested? No, not at all. I really don't know where you might be getting that idea. Outside of this specific project issue—the sabotage we've been discussing—my life is completely normal. I am still functioning at exactly the same high level I always have. 

I still translate, obviously. I still manage my team’s workflow, which, let me tell you, takes a considerable amount of energy and organization. I have to make sure the glossaries are distributed, the style guides are being strictly adhered to by the junior translators, the client deadlines are met... I do all of that just fine, day in and day out. 

And in my personal life, it's the exact same story. I'm not withdrawing or hiding away in a dark room somewhere. I pay the bills on time, I keep the household running, I keep up with all my family routines. We still do our usual weekend outings, I still read, I still keep up with international news—which is absolutely vital for my job, anyway. I haven't lost interest in a single one of those things. I'm as engaged with my family and my usual activities as I ever was.

The only place things really go off track, the only time my focus has to shift away from those normal, everyday things, is when the file history comes up. Or when I have to interact with certain coworkers, like the one I mentioned who sits in the breakroom. When that happens, yes, I have to drop what I'm doing and pay very, very close attention to the server logs, because if I don't, that's when they slip things through. That's when the translation memories get corrupted. So if I seem preoccupied to anyone, it's strictly localized to those specific triggers. It's not some general loss of interest in life, Doctor. It's just a necessary, targeted reallocation of my time and attention to protect my career from these people.
Did this problem at work begin suddenly?

Suddenly? Well, I suppose that depends entirely on how you define "suddenly," doesn't it? If you mean did I wake up one Tuesday and find everything completely upended, then no, not exactly. But if you mean was there a specific point in time where the baseline shifted, where the professional environment changed from standard competitive pressure to... to this coordinated campaign of sabotage, then yes, there was a definite starting point. 

This whole ordeal, this... this targeted tampering with my work, it's been going on for about 11 months now. I can pinpoint it almost exactly because it started shortly after I was put in charge of the new localization project for our biggest European client. 

You see, before that, I was handling a lot of the standard corporate communications—press releases, internal memos, that sort of thing. High volume, but relatively low stakes in terms of technical terminology. But this new project, the one I took over 11 months ago, it was a massive software UI localization. It required a very specific, highly technical glossary, and it was highly visible to upper management. I was selected to lead it because of my background, and I think... well, I know, that ruffled some feathers. Certain colleagues felt they should have been given the lead. 

So, it wasn't an overnight explosion of problems, but rather a very swift, very noticeable escalation that began right after that promotion—or reassignment, really. At first, it was just small things, a misplaced tag in the translation memory, a term that didn't match the approved glossary. Things you might initially write off as a careless error by a junior translator. But within a few weeks of me taking over that specific project, the "errors" became too frequent, too precise, and too damaging to just be accidental. They were specifically targeting the strings I had personally finalized. So, yes, 11 months of this. 11 months of constantly having to look over my shoulder and check the version history on every single file I touch.
For at least the last 3 months, have you continuously believed your coworkers were sabotaging your work?

Well, yes, absolutely continuously. I mean, it hasn't stopped for a single day. I’m here because for months—many months now, well past three—I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It's not a one-off thing, Doctor, it's a relentless, ongoing campaign. 

I log into the system, and I can see where certain subcontractors, and specifically that one colleague I mentioned earlier, keep making these... these tiny, insidious changes to the translation memory. They alter the timestamps, they tweak a tag here, they swap an approved term for a deprecated one there... and they do it in a way that makes it look exactly like my quality control failed. Like I was the one who missed it or approved the error. 

And the most frustrating part—the part that really proves how sophisticated this is—is that when I bring it up, when I demand an investigation and IT gets involved, they look at the logs and tell me the audit trail is clean. They say, "Oh, it shows you made the final commit," or "The system doesn't show any unauthorized access." But I know what I wrote. I know my own work. Even when IT says the record is clean, I know for an absolute fact that the digital record has been deliberately arranged, manipulated behind the scenes, specifically to put the blame on me. They are covering their tracks perfectly on the server side, but they can't hide the fact that the linguistic output is being sabotaged. So, yes, continuously. Every single day I have to brace myself for what they've altered overnight.
Has anyone told you that your speech or behavior has become noticeably disorganized or hard to follow?

Disorganized? Hard to follow? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, quite the opposite, really. If anything, I've been told I'm too meticulous, too precise in how I lay things out. 

You have to understand, Doctor, my entire profession—my entire adult life, really—is built around clarity. As a translator, and especially managing a team of translators, if my communication is disorganized, the entire project fails. I have to be incredibly precise about terminology, about syntax, about the exact nuance of a phrase in one language versus another. I spend my days writing detailed style guides, explaining exactly why a certain term must be used in a specific context, outlining the exact workflow for the QA process... You simply cannot do that if your thoughts are disorganized or your speech is hard to follow.

And even when I'm explaining this situation with my coworkers, this... this sabotage... I lay it out very logically. I mean, I have the timestamps, I have the version histories—or at least, I have my notes on what the version histories *should* look like before they manipulate the logs. When I go to HR or when I try to explain it to IT, I don't just rant and rave. I present a chronological sequence of events. I say, "On Tuesday at 4:00 PM, I finalized this string. On Wednesday at 9:00 AM, the string was altered, yet the system shows no log-in from the subcontractor who I know was assigned to review that section." I present it as a clear, undeniable pattern. 

Now, do they always *listen*? Do they always follow the logic? Well, that's a different story entirely. Sometimes I think HR deliberately plays dumb because they don't want to deal with the headache of a formal investigation. Or IT just looks at the surface-level server logs and refuses to dig deeper into the database architecture where the real tampering is happening. They might say, "We don't understand what you're getting at," but that's not because I'm being disorganized. That's because they are either willfully ignorant or simply lack the technical linguistic background to grasp the subtlety of what's being done to the translation memories. 

But as for my actual speech, my behavior, my ability to hold a conversation or explain a complex concept? No, no one has ever accused me of being hard to follow. I pride myself on being exceedingly clear. I have to be, just to survive in that environment right now.
Have you become emotionally flat or less expressive than you used to be?

Emotionally flat? Less expressive? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, if anything, I'm probably more expressive now than I used to be, just out of sheer frustration. 

You see, before all of this started—before the localization project and the tampering—I was always a very even-keeled person. In my line of work, you have to be. Interpreting, translating, it requires a certain professional detachment. You're a conduit for someone else's words, someone else's intent. You can't let your own emotions color the text. So, yes, I've always maintained a very professional, composed demeanor in the office. I'm not the type to, you know, shout or throw things or burst into tears at my desk. 

But lately? With this constant, insidious sabotage? It's impossible not to react. I mean, how would you feel if you poured hours of meticulous work into a highly technical glossary, carefully cross-referencing every term, only to log in the next morning and find that someone has systematically replaced all your approved terminology with deprecated, confusing jargon? And then, to add insult to injury, when you point it out, everyone just shrugs and looks at you like you're the one making a mistake? 

It's infuriating! And I don't hide that frustration. When I go to HR, I'm passionate. I'm animated. I lay out the evidence—the timestamps, the altered tags, the sheer impossibility of these errors happening by chance—and I demand action. I don't just sit there like a stone wall. I express my anger, my concern for the project's integrity, my absolute disbelief that they're allowing this to happen right under their noses. 

So, no, I haven't become flat or unexpressive. I'm very much alive, very much engaged, and very much determined to expose what they're doing. If anything, they're probably the ones who are emotionally flat—just sitting there, blank-faced, pretending they don't see the obvious pattern of sabotage I'm laying out right in front of them. It's like talking to a brick wall sometimes, I swear. But me? No, I'm expressing exactly how I feel about this whole nightmare.
Before this problem at work began, had you ever had a similar experience of being targeted or plotted against?

No, no, never. Honestly, Doctor, that is exactly what makes this entire situation so incredibly baffling—and so devastating, frankly. Before I took on this specific localization project, I had never experienced anything even remotely like this. Not once. 

I mean, if you look at my career history... I’ve been an interpreter and translator for well over a decade, ever since I finished my graduate program. I’ve worked with multiple agencies, I’ve handled high-stakes corporate accounts, complex technical manuals, you name it. And in all those environments, across all those years, I always had fantastic working relationships. Sure, you have your normal professional disagreements—maybe a debate with an editor over whether a certain idiom translates better literally or figuratively, or a minor dispute with a project manager about a tight turnaround time—but it was always professional. It was always above board, out in the open. 

I have never, ever had anyone actively try to undermine my work before. I’ve never felt targeted or plotted against. I've always trusted my colleagues completely. We were a team, working toward a shared goal of linguistic accuracy. So, you know, if I were just the kind of person who naturally assumed people were out to get me, wouldn't I have had those issues at my last firm? Or during my master's degree? But I didn't. My track record is impeccable. I've always been respected. 

It’s only *this* group, *this* specific project, where the environment has turned so deliberately toxic and... and conspiratorial. That’s why I'm so certain about what's happening in the server logs now, because I have my entire past career as a baseline for what normal, healthy collaboration looks like. I know what a genuine mistake looks like versus intentional tampering, because for my whole adult life, I've only ever dealt with honest mistakes. So to answer your question, no. Nothing like this has ever happened to me before. This coordinated campaign against me is entirely unprecedented.
Have you ever felt that outside forces were controlling your actions or movements?

Controlling my actions? Like... like physically moving my body or forcing me to do things? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I am in complete control of myself at all times. My mind is my own, my movements are my own. When I sit down at my desk, when I place my hands on the keyboard, I am the one deciding every single keystroke. I choose the words, I choose the syntax, I hit the enter key. 

Actually, that's exactly why this whole situation with the localization project is so incredibly frustrating to me. Because I *know* what I did. I know exactly what actions I took. If some... some outside force were controlling my hands, well, maybe then I could understand how a perfectly good, meticulously translated string suddenly gets reverted to a completely nonsensical, outdated mess overnight. If I were being puppeted around, I might say, 'Oh, well, I didn't have control over that.' But that's just science fiction, isn't it? No one is moving my arms like a marionette. 

I make my own choices. I choose when to log into the portal, I choose what terminology to apply from the master glossary, I choose when to draft an email to the project manager detailing the discrepancies. Every action I take is deliberate and fully my own. The issue isn't that my actions are being controlled. The issue is that *after* I take an action—my own, fully conscious, deliberate action—someone else comes in and alters the digital footprint of that action on the backend. Do you see the distinction there? It’s not about my movements, it’s about them manipulating the work after the fact to make it look like I'm incompetent. 

So, no, to answer your question, I have never felt like anything or anyone was controlling my actions or my movements. I am entirely in the driver's seat of my own body, Doctor. Always have been.
